Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj is raising a substantial problem which I cannot settle right now because I don't have all the necessary information but his argument is as follows: He says that he'd been informed, under Rule 68(i) of the fact that there were 206.000 pages of documents that might be exculpatory material, but that the Prosecution, as they realised it was impossible to disclose 260 pages in hard copy and moreover to disclose them in B/C/S, actually sort of shifts that material in 68(ii), actually shifts a great majority of those documents under (ii) so that he's forced to search them electronically. That's what he claims. I don't know. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We disagree. I'm looking at the disclosure log records of the material that was tendered to him and the receipts, and the rule change created subcategories, and a lot of the disclosure that was tendered in electronic form predates the rule change or is not differentiated between 68(i) and 68(ii) and what I've explained is the nature of electronic collections is that they are dependent on the quality of the data and the efficiency and efficacy of the search engine. If Mr. Seselj wants to see the disks that were tendered to him in electronic form with a label of Rule 68, he is welcome to have them. He has refused them. The passage of time means -- and the improvements to the electronic -- if I may just quickly, I want to make sure there is no misunderstanding is if we have documents that are disclosable under Rule 68(i) we will give them to him in -- or have given them to him with that label in the format required by the Court. But the passage of time means that if I were to run the very same search terms today, I would have a better search result, and if we have material that's within our actual knowledge that falls within the ruling of the Chamber to put it in Serbian and give it to him in paper that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The advantage of this contradictory system, this adversarial system, is to highlight a number of issues and I'm discovering something new. You've just said that under Rule 68, you did disclose to Mr. Seselj, who came to The Hague in 2003, a number of documents, and then you are right in saying that Rule 68 was amended. This was amended on the 21st of July 2004 -- 28th of July. I remember this took place at the plenary session and the rule was amended. The distinction was made between what is communicated in hard copy and what is disclosed in electronic format. And in your submission, you are saying that what had been provided in electronic format before was still being disclosed electronically, and it's only after the 28th of July 2004, that you are under the obligation to disclose in hard copy anything that comes under Rule 68(i). Is this how I should understand what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Not precisely, Your Honour, and I'm approaching the problem pragmatically from a different direction. I am looking at the change in the disclosure requirements that the Chamber has ruled to adapt and effectuate Mr. Seselj's right of self-representation and I'm looking at the fact that we have prior disclosure that doesn't have the label.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, just a minute. The decision taken by the Trial Chamber, which one are you talking about? One decision was taken during the pre-trial phase and then was handed down by Trial Chamber I and the Trial Chamber that was supposed to try him and then by Trial Chamber III, notwithstanding the decisions taken by the Chambers I am under the obligation of compliance with the rules, and Rule 68, as it stands, I think. You have provided an explanation. I think I understand where problem stems from. Out of these 206.000 pages that have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj, this has been disclosed electronically initially. And this is what Mr. Seselj is challenging. And you are saying, yes, but Rule 68 was amended on the 28th of July 2004, and this amendment means that anything that had been disclosed electronically could remain that way, but now, as far as Rule 68(i) is concerned, you now have to disclose material in hard copy. I don't think I have misrepresented what you have said, have I?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The qualification is that the receipts or the materials that labelled the electronic collections previously described indicate the search terms and produce a body of electronically held evidence in conjunction with the ability to look at it. The receipts don't indicate whether it's Rule 68(i) or Rule 68(ii) which I think for purposes of ensuring compliance with the orders of this Court in June 2007, I need to make sure that he has -- Mr. Seselj has received in paper, in Serbian, everything under Rule 68(i). I can't recreate those disks and then decide, is it -- which paragraph it falls under. If he wants to use the old disks, they are available to him. What I'm saying is that with the rules as they stand now, if we have material within our knowledge that falls within Rule 68(i), it will be disclosed per the orders of the Chamber in the appropriate format to facilitate his preparation of his defence. Because of the nature of electronic evidence, evidence held in electronic format, I won't get the same results, I'll get a better set of results, frankly, if I run the same search terms again but I consider that those materials under the old rules that were provided without differentiation of whether it was simply material relevant to the preparation or under the more narrow consideration of exculpatory, that label can't be superimposed on this material and to do so would produce an erroneous result and I don't want it to be misrepresented that there is 400.000 pages of exculpatory material. That's simply not true. If I were to count the number of pages that truly contradict our theory of the case, they are extremely small and they have been disclosed with the appropriate labelling so that we have brought them to his attention as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I shall give you the floor, but I was going to say that the ball is in your court, because these 206.000 documents have been disclosed to you in electronic form -- in an electronic format before Rule 68 was amended on the 28th of July 2004. The Prosecution was working along those lines. In June 2007 I handed down a decision stating that on the basis of these documents, the Prosecution was under the obligation to disclose in hard copy all the documents that come under Rule 68(i). And the Prosecution says that it has complied with its obligation, and the Prosecution adds that under Rule 68(i), there are not thousands of documents, they are just a few documents. That is true. As a rule, if there were thousands of documents, it would be difficult to understand that we have an indictment. You can't have an indictment if we have a whole series of exhibits that suggest the innocence of the accused. So the Prosecution has said, after having selected the documents, they have indicated to you which documents come, strictly speaking, under Rule 68(i) and which documents are those documents which should be disclosed to you in hard copy and in Serbian. As you know, it is the Prosecution who states that this is -- it comes under Rule 68(i) or under Rule 68(ii), and the Prosecution may feel that this is not exculpatory material. So this is what the problem hinges on. You may have made a mistake, Mr. Seselj, and you may believe that these 206.000 documents all come under Rule 68(i).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I think it's high time you impose certain sanctions on counsel for the Prosecution because she is consciously deceiving you in relation to certain facts. You yourself have stated that the rule was changed on the 28th of July 2004, and then this was introduced under Roman (ii), as far as I can recall. Those 207.000 documents under Rule 68, they tried to hand those to me on the 30th of September 2004, a full two months after the rule was changed, and let me draw your attention to one more point, which is my crucial piece of evidence that they are consciously deceiving you. Rule 68(i) refers to disclosure of evidence, to make the distinction as clear as possible, whereas Rule 68(ii) makes available a collection of relevant documents. This is not disclosure of evidence. It is simply the Prosecutor's obligation to make available to me relevant collections of material so that I myself might possibly find a document I might find useful which they have not noticed. And that is an essential difference. In this paper of the 6th of November, actually it was delivered to you on the 2nd of November, it says clearly Rule 68 disclosure of evidence. What evidence? Potentially exculpatory evidence. It doesn't say here access to collections of documents. It refers to disclosure of evidence, 207.000 pages of relevant -- of relevant exculpatory evidence exists. I know what I've been accused of. There have been hundreds of pages of potentially exculpatory material in other cases too. This was material that a representative of the OTP thought at some point that it might be exculpatory but it might be not. It's up to me to decide how to use this material, and whether to use it or not, but I must have it available. These 207.000 pages do not refer to collections of materials which I might search. These are 207.000 pages of evidence. What kind of evidence? Potentially exculpatory evidence. So don't allow them to continue deceiving us in this way. They have to fulfil their obligations. Last year, they made a mistake in admitting that those 207.000 pages exist, and now they want to retract this. They want to withdraw, they want to eliminate this and I will not allow it. Their collections of relevant material contain millions of pages. Their collections of relevant material contain all the documentary material which is not under an embargo, as far as I'm concerned. There might be materials which they do not want to disclose to me because they refer to protected witnesses or documents protected in other cases, but what they could make available to me is millions of pages of their collections of documents. This has nothing to do with 68(i), the disclosure of evidence. It says here, Rule 68, disclosure of evidence. It's potentially exculpatory evidence. This evidence has to be disclosed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj has just made a series of comments which require my attention. As far as the table of disclosed documents is concerned. Now, Rule 68, on the 9th of February 2004, the accused has received 274 pages in B/C/S, 163 in English, in a CD format which he refused. But I realise that no distinction has been made between (i) and (ii). Then on the second of February 2004 he has been given documents which he accepted in hard copy. Then on the 7th, on the 24th of May 2004, namely before the Plenary Session, he was given documents which he accepted. So the only problem with page 1 is item 5, which indicates that he did not accept the documents. On the 8th and the 9th, for item 8 and 9, on the 3rd of September 2004, in other words, after the Plenary Session, after the session, the distinction had been made between (i) and (ii) and 18.000 pages had been disclosed to Mr. Seselj in electronic form, and Mr. Seselj did not accept the latter. Any legal expert in his first year of training understands that the distinction must be made between the (i) and the little (i). Item 10, on the 30th of September you disclose a CD containing 207.000 pages, and that's where the problem lies. Why are there 207.000 pages that have been disclosed? Does this come under the (i) or the (ii), the first or the second paragraph of Rule 68? Because - I'm going to give you the floor because I'd just like to finish - you were under the obligation in September 2004 to disclose to the accused in hard copies anything coming under Rule 68(i) and you sent this to him in electronic format. On the 27th of November, same thing happens, but he receives a piece of paper and accepts it. But he, on the 28th of January, he is being given 343 pages and a number of pages in B/C/S. He does not accept it because it is sent in a CD form. On the 23rd of September 2005, he receives the 14 statements which he accepts because these were sent in hard copy. On the 11th of October, 2005, a number of documents are sent back because they were only partially translated from what I understand, and this was sent in hard copy. And I'm going to finish with this. There are still a few left. On the 5th of April 2006, he accepts hard copy documents, so that's not a problem. On the 29th of June, he accepts a number of hard copy documents. That's not a problem. On the 25th of September, we encounter a problem because it's Mr. Hooper who signs the receipt, and this is a CD which contains a number of interviews, 75 pages of various statements, 68(i), 68(ii), I don't know which part of the rule these come under. Then on the 16th of October 2006, Mr. Hooper receives one page, I don't know what this means, and then lastly, on the 19th of October, Mr. Hooper signs the receipt for 50 pages. We don't know whether it comes under (i) or (ii). So the problem occurs for item 10 where on the 30th of September 2004 he received 207.000 documents. I'd like to understand what is happening here. Does this come under (i) or (ii), the first or the second paragraph of Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: There is an error in the premise of your question, Your Honour. Until the decision of June 7, 2007, there was no obligation on -- held by the Prosecution to disclose to Mr. Seselj in paper form. To the contrary, the decision of 4 July 2006 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree with you, Ms. Dahl. The rule was amended on the 28th of July 2004. The rule stipulates that the Prosecutor provides any material which might be of an exculpatory nature to the accused, and this is done the way it should, since the inception of this Tribunal, in hard copy. But I attended the Plenary Session, so a discussion followed at the Plenary Session, as there are other documents that could be of interest to the accused, the accused can then ask to have these documents. In that case, this can be forwarded in electronic -- in an electronic form. This is the tenor of Rule 68. This is why, when the decision was taken in June, I asked you to forward any exculpatory material in hard copy coming under paragraph (i). There is no mistake in the premise here. I took part in the vote.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, your view of Rule 68(i) is not generally shared and is in fact contrary to the decision of Trial Chamber I on 4 July 2007 which authorised the Prosecution to make disclosure in electronic form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have nothing to do with Trial Chamber I any more. We now have a new Chamber, and I have full powers and so I order you to disclose to Mr. Seselj any exculpatory material coming under Rule 68(i).

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... out of these 207.000 documents, that's five, 10, 20, 30, I don't know, it's for you to select these documents, and to disclose them to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We understand what the obligation is and the ruling of the Trial Chamber. The point that I think there is still disagreement is whether our prior attempts to discharge our obligations were in compliance with the rules. And they were in strict compliance with the orders of the Trial Chamber that were upheld as a matter of law by the Appeals Chamber. And we respect that this Chamber has taken a different view under its authority to manage the trial and we are endeavouring to make sure that we have disclosed everything required by this Trial Chamber in the form that you have spelled out. You're asking me to go back in time and make a declaration as to the nature of documents that were disclosed in electronic form. That I cannot do. And frankly, to spend precious resources in a forensic expedition into these disks does not serve the fact that we need to move forward in the disclosure and make sure that material that is under Rule 68(i) is disclosed in a timely manner. I can't add labels to receipts that aren't there, and I have a different set of software and a different set of evidence that has been improved with the ongoing improvements in technology. There is an entire electronic disclosure suite that is available to all accused in this Tribunal that is constantly being improved to ensure that people can find quickly relevant information and that resource is available to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think here we are talking about very crucial point, the rights of the accused. The accused is entitled to have access to any exculpatory material or any other documents. You are telling me now, and I am very fortunate to be the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, which means I can address these issues in detail, and you are telling me that you are unable to give Mr. Seselj those documents coming under Article -- Rule 68(i) because they are lost in a swathe of 207.000 documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That is not what I'm saying. I'm saying that if we have documents within our actual knowledge that fall within the remit of Rule 68(i) they will be disclosed but the prior disclosures of electronic collections under the name of Rule 68 did not differentiate between 68(i) and 68 little (i) and in looking for the search results --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't play on words, Ms. Dahl. On the 30th of September 2004, we have a CD-ROM which contains 207.010 pages. This CD-ROM on the 30th of September is stamped and comes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Comes under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of these 207.000 pages, how many pages actually come under Rule 68(i)? That's my question. That is the essence of the matter here. How many pages come under Rule 68(i), which at the rule means you should look at these 207.000 pages and forward them, and understand what comes under Rule 68(i) and (ii). I understand full well that you are limited by your resources and cannot do this. If that is the case, file a new motion with a view to reconsidering the decision that was taken in June, and Mr. Seselj will reply and say what he thinks about it. I then will confirm what I have already said, and you will ask the Appeals Chamber what needs to be done. But if we have a fair trial, the accused must have the documents, all documents, and we have these 207.000 pages. So either you're telling me that you did look at these 207.000 pages and you have disclosed to Mr. Seselj, pursuant to the decision we took in June, those pages that come under Rule 68(i) and then there is no problem whatsoever, and in that case, you need to be honest about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The documents are both inculpatory and exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You have asked a question that cannot be answered because of the passage of time. The receipt lists search terms and the disclosure effort produces a set of documents in electronic form that are responsive to the search terms. It is not a matter of reviewing documents page by page as we do in our trial preparation, and when we find something that comes under Rule 68(i) that we then disclose that to the accused with the appropriate indication. It is not permissible under the rules to simply unload a pile of documents without differentiation regarding the relevance of the material and we are not seeking to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, let's be clear. In the past, I had the same job as you have today. I know what this entails. What I would like to know is you have done the following: Based on the software packages you had, which contained these 207.000 pages, have you reviewed these 207.000 pages? Have they all been downloaded and have you checked them all out to make sure that you knew which documents came under Rule 68(i)? If that's been done for these 207.000 pages you just say so, and in that case, the documents which you have disclosed to Mr. Seselj are the outcome of this research work, and if that has not been done, you can say that this has been partially done or we haven't done this at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Those tasks are not involved in creating an electronic collection of material responsive to search terms. I have not had a staff of individuals reviewing every single page and first of all this is also three years ago as well. So I cannot stand here today and say that someone has turned a physical page and looked at each piece. The presumption is with electronic collections that the viewer knows what he's looking for, can initiate a search request and page through the responsive terms. These search terms came out of the Milosevic case. They relate to what is considered "perpetrating organisations." They refer to documents responsive to the search term "5th Military District", "9th Knin Corps", "Captain Dragan", "Civil Defence Croatia", "Colonel-General Andrija Raseta", "KOS", "Maritime Military District", "Martic's Police", "SAO Krajina Police", including "National Security Service", "Serbian Volunteer Guards", "VRS", and the "White Eagles." I believe, if we were to run the search terms again, we would get a more discrete set of documents and to review them for the sole purpose, to review the CDs for the sole purpose of indicating under which prong of the current rule they apply is inconsistent with the obligations under the rules. They are an electronic collection, they are now outdated because of improvements in technology. I think that it complies with the disclosure obligations as defined by this Trial Chamber that we disclose what is within our actual knowledge, in paper, in Serbian, that falls within Rule 68(i). I don't think that it is incumbent upon us to go back to electronic collections that were tendered to Mr. Seselj to differentiate what prong under the rules they apply. I think it is a better use of the resources of the Tribunal to carry those obligations under the current ability to search information in electronic format and to measure it against the current indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give you the floor in a minute, Mr. Seselj. You are right, there are the Tribunal's resources but there are also the rights of the accused. Let us imagine that among the documents there are exculpatory documents. In such an event somebody would be tried whilst there are documents likely to show he's innocent and we would just say oh, no, we couldn't do the work. That can't be done. You are telling me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that your people did this work. I want to make sure of one thing, that the 207.000 documents have been viewed. I suppose somebody is behind a screen or in front of a screen, runs a software and starts looking at documents and then they say, "Oh, this one is going to be disclosed." That's my concern. I want the documents to have been checked by the Prosecutor, upstream, so that the accused can at least be sure that the documents that might be beneficial to him have been listed by the Prosecutor. I am under the impression that you've started this work but it's not quite completed. That's not good enough for me. I want to make sure that all the documents under Rule 68(i) are in the possession of Mr. Seselj. That's my only goal. And I'm not going to fall back on costs or the number of staff working on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We are in complete agreement that Mr. Seselj should have all of the documents that fall within Rule 68(i). There is no disagreement about that. The process of investigating and assembling a body of evidence with which to prosecute an accused charged in this Tribunal includes systematic and thorough review of evidence in our collection. We review it to determine whether it tends to support the charges or exculpate the accused. When we find material that could be considered Rule 68(i), we disclose it. That is a separate function from creating a collection of evidence based on a Rule-based search used by a search engine and placed on CD. The Appeals Chamber in many decisions has said it is not proper to simply disclose a large volume of material without differentiating the relevance on it. It's not reasonable to expect a Defence team to look at that material one page at a time without any idea of why it's being disclosed. In this situation, there are collections that have been gathered of rule-based computer searches that are put on CD based on our looking at the theory of defence in Milosevic, Mr. Seselj's theory of defence here, and as I described before, perhaps the perpetrating organisations that might be relevant to preparation of the Defence. Unfortunately, the receipts for these CDs don't indicate under what prong the material was collected. But I want to draw an important distinction, when we find things, when human beings see something and understand its relevance as an exculpatory document, that gets disclosed. That is different than the exercise of gathering and making available to the Defence rule-based search results. Frankly, rule-based search results are better than human beings and sometimes they suffer from serious shortcomings because they are over-inclusive. In our preparation of the case, we review documents and make disclosure of what comes within our actual knowledge but I cannot say on these large collections of rule-based search results that I have had a staff member look at each single one. That is inconsistent with the use of rule-based computer search generated subsets of an evidence collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, first of all, I would like to point out to you a basic contradiction in what the counsel for the Prosecution said. She said just now, towards the end, that right now the Prosecutor cannot say what the nature of the documents is from 2004, that is, because at that time this Prosecutor was not involved in this case. However, I would like to remind you that at the beginning of the debate with regard to this issue, counsel for the Prosecution claimed that these 207.000 documents were delivered to me according to Rule 68(ii). I remind you of that. You can see it in the transcript. When I intervened and when I pointed out that there were two months in between, that is to say from the point in time when Rule 68 was changed until these documents were delivered, counsel for the Prosecution changed her position completely and then started talking about her problems. And before that, she was categorically prepared to assert that this was in accordance with 68(ii). I would like to point out the substantive difference between the disclosure of evidence and making available collections of relevant material that are to be searched. A few moments ago, counsel for the Prosecution mentioned certain categories of documents that are potentially exculpatory for me. For me, all of them are potentially exculpatory. The documents on the White Eagles for instance are very important because a large number of Muslim witnesses in their ignorance speak of Seselj's White Eagles whereas the basic premise of my Defence that I never ever had anything to do with these White Eagles. Then a large number of Prosecution witnesses ascribed to me crimes of the Serb Guards of Vuk Draskovic. The basic premise of my Defence is that where Vuk Draskovic's Serb Guards operated not a single crime can be linked to me. When Bijeljina was within the indictment many witnesses ascribed to me Arkan's and Mauzer's crimes. In Zvornik, what they ascribed to me are the crimes of the Yellow Wasps. Therefore all the material about the Serb Guards, the White Eagles, Arkan's men, the Yellow Wasps are potentially exculpatory materials for me. I'm not surprised in the least that there is 207.000 pages of potentially exculpatory documents. That is what existed in all other cases or a bit less or a bit more. However, now, the Prosecution is in trouble and I understand their trouble because now they have to put all of this on paper. The Prosecution is right. Before, the Trial Chambers involved looked upon this kindly. That is to say, their behaviour regarding documents. That made them complacent. They thought that this was a fait accompli. Now it turned out that this is not a fait accompli at all and that they actually have to disclose all of these potentially exculpatory documents on paper. We are not talking about some documents from among the 207.000 documents. All 207.000 documents of potentially exculpatory documents are there. There is not a single document there among these hundreds of thousands of pages that is not potentially exculpatory for me. That is what I assert. Whoever did this in the OTP did not disclose to me, as evidence, something that simply could have made it possible for me to do my own search. They made their own selection, according to their own criteria, seeing whether something was potentially exculpatory or not. This selection was carried out and the result of this selection that this person made is 207.000 pages. Now, I seek to see these 207.000 pages. That's the point of it. And if you allow me I'd like to say a few more things about what we discussed just before the break so I deal with it straight away. This is the first time I hear that on the 25th of June the Prosecution submitted a request to amend the indictment. I have not received that yet. I expect this to be translated into the Serbian language. Perhaps I'm going to wait for about a month for that, as I've been waiting for other documents too. I would like to remind you of the following, Judge. Once I receive the Serb translation, I have the right to respond to the request to amend the indictment. And then the Trial Chamber rules on the potential amendment of the indictment and when the Trial Chamber makes its decision, then the Prosecution submits to me supporting material for this new amended indictment. And once they submit that material to me, I have another month to object. And then, when I object, and if this is refused, then I have the right to appeal, and what am I going to appeal on? Challenging jurisdiction. The question is whether the trial can start in that case, even in March next year. I would like to draw your attention to this so that you bear this in mind when you make your ultimate decision as to whether you will allow them to amend the indictment or not. Secondly, if an amendment indictment is approved, then in the supporting material, I have to be given the entire Appeals judgement from the Brdjanin case, because if I understand you correctly the backbone of the amendments to the indictment is based on the treatment of joint criminal enterprise in the appeal judgement in Brdjanin which I have never seen. I have to see that before I submit my own motion regarding the indictment. So this extends the deadline for starting the trial even further. What is the objective? I don't know. I can only estimate what the objective is. Perhaps somebody is hoping that the mandate of the Tribunal will be extended and that my trial can go on until 2020, but I do know that Mr. Churkin, the ambassador of Russia to the United Nations, stated in the Security Council that there is no reason whatsoever to extend the mandate and the work of the Tribunal and I believe that Russia is going to adhere to that position. And without the consent of Russia there can be no extension and do not count on that, the fact that my trial has not been completed, the work of the Tribunal is going to be extended. No way. My right to have a trial within a reasonable time limit has been violated irreparably. There is no way of remedying that. Now I would like to focus on ruling out the possibility of violating my other procedural rights. I'll wait. I'll wait until 2020 if my health is still good. I have the patience to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, several things. One minor point, one not so minor, but compared to the substantive issue, it is secondary, albeit important. Mr. Seselj has just said that the amended indictment had not been disclosed to him. I guess it's been sent to be translated and he hasn't yet received it in his own language. This being said, I hope he'll receive it shortly. Secondly, the amended indictment is one of the by-products of the Brdjanin appeal decision, so at the very least he should have in his own language the translation of the relevant passages on JCE. That's the least one can expect. That shouldn't pose a problem. However, I've been listening to both of you, and I was struck by one thing. By what Mr. Seselj said on the White Eagles, the Yellow Wasps, and the -- and Arkan's men. He's just said this to us. He argues that he didn't know these people, that they were not under his orders or authority, and in his view, if there are any documents that are part of the 207.000 pages about these people, he should have them because he said these are potentially exculpatory documents. So this is what he claims. I don't know. But it is for the Prosecution to check. I can understand, Ms. Dahl, you're not responsible for that yourself, you followed colleagues who themselves followed each other in this case and you arrived recently and you discovered all this recently. But as a rule, when the Prosecution goes to court, in order to introduce evidence because the Prosecution has the onus of proof, the Prosecution is supposed to know all the documents, and I, if I were you, if I wanted to go to court, to go to trial, I would feel that I would have to know myself the 207.000 pages, I do not want to run the risk of going to court without first having seen the documents. So that's it. I know that in our cases, there are thousands, if not millions, of pages involved but as a rule, the Prosecution is supposed to know the documents, is supposed, according to the rules, to sort out the documents, to select them. So that's the reality. And equally, the Defence is supposed to be aware of the Prosecution and Defence evidence, is supposed to know their own Defence case. Of course, this issue is not going to be solved today but I do draw your attention to the fact that the accused has just claimed that there are documents in the 207.000 pages concerning groups or individuals, could be exculpatory, if he were to be apprised of them, so this is a substantive problem obviously in September when this chart was disclosed as a CD, it must have been prepared prior to the 28th of January 2004, all these questions had not been totally understood and they crop up now. You must think it over. I, for my part, will see what I can do at my level, but I have just identified a problem, which could prevent us from starting the trial. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to thank Mr. Seselj for indicating areas of this case which he considers to be exculpatory. We will take that under advisement and initiate commission searches to identify material that he considers exculpatory and falling within our disclosure obligations. That is helpful information so that we can discharge our disclosure obligations. With regard to delays associated with accommodating Mr. Seselj's right to represent himself, we do not consider that these delays render the proceedings unfair. To the contrary, they represent the effort to give meaning to his right to self-represent. With respect to citations to the Brdjanin appeals judgement, we are preparing a book of authorities that will include the excerpts that we consider relevant. We thought that that would assist in the translation of relevant legal materials to facilitate his preparation. When we cite material before the Appeals Chamber that's outside our jurisprudence we regularly prepare a book of authorities for Chambers and we thought it would be appropriate to assist Mr. Seselj in getting his hands around the jurisprudence that we offer that same preparation in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me address very briefly something else because I'm going to have another trial this afternoon, and I do wish to address this problem now. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution filed a pre-trial brief. It is filed as being confidential for the time being, and it is several pages long. I am not going to speak to its contents. I only wanted to flag to you that when there is a pre-trial brief, you are entitled to supply a response, your own brief. You can decide to do so or not to do so but this pre-trial brief is, as it were, a very developed indictment, in which all the arguments, all the Prosecution's arguments are developed. I glanced at it, and having done so, I believe that you have tools that make it possible for you to respond to the allegations contained in the pre-trial brief. But this is a major piece of work, if you intend to carry it out. So far, it has never been done. I'll tell you the exact number of pages of this pre-trial brief, 74 pages, and there are 599 footnotes. Of course, this pre-trial brief will have to be translated in your own language, and once you have read it, studied it, you will be free to respond to it, which is actually your Defence case as set out, as you would set out in your pre-trial brief. I do invite you to read this pre-trial brief, to really look into it. Of course, subject to further decisions on the indictment. What I'm saying now is provided the indictment remains the same. If the indictment were to be quashed or amended later on, that would be another problem but we already have a document based on the current indictment. You could usefully prepare your defence in writing a pre-trial brief because you basically have the Prosecution case in their pre-trial brief. See if you can supply your own pre-trial brief. I suggest you do. If you fail to do so it's up to you. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I will certainly respond to the pre-trial brief using the same number of pages that the Prosecution used. I think that is my right and I think that is what you will grant to me. Secondly, you know the kind of problems I'm facing now. I am waiting for the decision to arrive, perhaps it will arrive today, allowing me to object to the modified reduced indictment. You informed me last time that you made that decision. However, it hasn't been submitted to me yet. I have the right within a month to object to that, and I will certainly do that. Then, I have the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, which is based on that indictment. I'm going to respond to that as well and I think that you gave me one month's deadline for that too. And I'm going to respond to that as well. Then, if you decide to admit the new amended indictment, then I am going to respond to that and then the new pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, then I have the right to respond to that new pre-trial brief for the Prosecution, practically we are starting things all over again. I'm not going to give up on any one of my procedural rights. But I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that all my procedural rights are renewed with this new indictment and that is going to require a great deal of time, and a great deal of effort. I do not fear the effort. But as for the time, you will have to think about that. So I am not shying away from this new indictment. I'm not opposing it in advance before I see what it's all about. First, I'm going to look at it, then I'm going to object. As for the current document that is being prepared in view of the existing indictment, it's being prepared by my legal advisers, it is going to be based on two things, challenging hate speech as a form of committing a crime, and challenging the way in which parts of the indictment were chosen for reduction, for elimination. I already told you that we are going to insist that instead of Bijeljina, Samac, Western Slavonia, et cetera, Vojvodina be eliminated because in that case, it is more than obvious that this trial cannot have jurisdiction because there is no nexus to the armed conflicts and there was no attack against the civilian population. The members of my expert team have been charged with preparing a special study about this and we are going to file that as well. If you think that this is too much you can simply reject it but in this additional study we will try to indicate to you all the evidence supporting our position that the problems that may have occurred in Vojvodina cannot be the subject of this indictment and this international court cannot have jurisdiction over that, and there was no widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. There was no attack against the civilian population. There were sporadic interethnic incidents for various reasons but you're going to see all of that from this paper that we will be submitting, so the basic thesis of my Defence is that it is not appropriate as far as what the Trial Chamber insisted upon is concerned, this reduction was not appropriate. And the first point has to do with another point that I wanted to object to, and that is hate speech that the Prosecution introduced as a new form of committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point of clarification. I will certainly read with a keen interest what you will say about Vojvodina and I shall never reject any written submissions if they have to do with the rights of the accused to a fair trial. If you go beyond the word count or number of pages, you should do what your associates do: You should in an introductory paragraph ask for a waiver because that is an important question. But as far as I'm concerned I shall never dismiss a document because it -- the number of pages is too great. Justice must prevail and we need to be able to look at the documents coming from both parties. This is what I had to say about this particular matter. As this is a Status Conference, I need to turn to you and ask you if healthwise, everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as detention matters are concerned, are your conditions of detention appropriate? You have no complaints to lodge or you're not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to the conditions of detention but I would like to advise you that for almost five years, the Registry has been applying discriminatory measures towards me. I am the only detainee who does not have the right to invite his friends for a visit. I am able to receive visits only from my closest family and two authorised representatives of the Serb Radical Party, and my legal advisers and case manager. All the other detainees have the right to also invite their friends to visit them and many have whole processions of friends passing through the visiting room, but in my case, Registry has always rejected any application from me, saying that-- and giving as an excuse that these are all members of the Serb Radical Party and that I have two official representatives of the Serb Radical Party visiting me. But all my friends are members of the Serb Radical Party. These are the people I socialise with, the people I am friends with, and they are now being disqualified from visiting me only because they are members of the Serb Radical Party and this maltreatment has been going on for five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew nothing about this. The fact that you're being prevented from seeing friends, who happen to be members of your political party. Has a decision been taken on this matter? Has a ruling been made?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the case of my application to have Igor Becic visit me. This was refused by the Registry saying that he is a deputy of the Serb Radical Party. Then I appealed to the President of the Tribunal who rejected my appeal. That's a specific example. There have been several other examples too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, then file a motion and send me a motion. File a motion which you submit to the Chamber and explain why this person was prevented from seeing you, and what ties unite you, and how the situation stands with the other accused. There is no reason why you should be discriminated. This is something new to me. It's not because you are a member of any political party that people are being prevented from seeing you. So please file a motion and I shall issue a decision. Ms. Dahl, is there any other subject which you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to adjourn soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I wanted to -- I had several questions that arose out of the setting of a trial date. We need a firm trial date both for logistical and security reasons, as I'm sure you have tremendous experience with the challenges associated with bringing international witnesses in and ensuring proper preparation for their testimony and making the disclosures required to assist the Defence in its preparation. So that is first, that a firm trial date obviously with all of the information discussed today, it may be beyond our reach at this point. Nevertheless, in preparing the order of witnesses and estimating time for testimony, I would appreciate if the Court were able to quantify for me the meaning of a three -- of sitting three days a week, and what I need to know in planning purposes is the number of hours sitting three days a week means so that I can realistically put together a schedule for the witnesses, giving due consideration to the form of their testimony and taking into consideration the relevance and grouping the evidence according to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall respond straight away. This is precisely why I asked you to give me your schedule, and with your estimated time, you estimate the time you need for each witness and then I shall look at the schedule and compare it with the 65 ter list of witnesses, and look into its relevance. And then I shall set a number of hours, but in order to do so, I need to have your schedule. Are you going to call 50 witnesses, 60 witnesses? I don't know. You are the only person who knows this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would refer the Court to our 65 ter list that does contain an estimated duration of testimony as well as a form of testimony that is producing that estimation, that was filed on 29 March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, I've been working for four years in this Tribunal and I must tell you that the 65 ter lists are always quite optimistic because the Prosecution calls a -- provides a number of names on these lists but does not always call all the witnesses. I would like you to work honestly. I would like your schedule to reflect the witnesses you really intend to call to testify, and we then see where we stand because, as I told you last time, if we are talking about a particular municipality, if initially you intended to call ten witnesses, you could call two viva voce witnesses, two 92 ter witnesses and then perhaps a few 92 bis witnesses to corroborate what the previous ones have said but you have to make quite sure you know which viva voce witnesses you wish to call to testify as well as the 92 ter witnesses. So this preparatory work needs to be done and you may then tell me I need 200 hours or 300 hours; I honestly don't know. And from then on, the Defence also says that 300 hours is enough or not enough, and then the Chamber can rule on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The piece of information I'm needing to make this schedule and this estimation is how many hours on a particular day one would anticipate hearing evidence. That will allow me within a one week period to try to group or a three-day -- three-day trial sitting that I can group. If I know it's a four-hour day or six-hour day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally speaking, we have decided that we would sit on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, each hearing lasts four hours to four and a half hours, but this really amounts to four hours, so that could be -- you would have 12 hours a week. But out of these 12 hours, of course, half of this is accounted for by cross-examination. So you would only all in all have six hours a week, six hours for you and six hours for Mr. Seselj. So per week, which means that would be six multiplied by four, that would amount to 24 hours a month, and over a period of ten months, you would have 240 hours but out of a period -- over a period of ten months, that would be too long. Mr. Seselj would then have ten months and this trial is due to last two years so this is not possible. So you would have to rather go for 120 hours. I don't know what estimated figure was given to you by the previous Trial Chamber but basically your examination time should last or should take something between 120 and 150 hours. This is a rough estimate. In that case, Mr. Seselj would have the same time, i.e., something ranging from 120 to 150 hours so in an ideal situation, the trial should take place in 2008. This is why I said that November seemed an appropriate time but Mr. Seselj has submitted a number of problems to us today, and as far as he's concerned, he feels that March would be a more appropriate time to commence this trial. All of this needs to be reviewed. We have to understand what the Prosecution is going to do, what is going to happen to the various documents, but you can already -- already start working along these lines, something between 120 hours and 150 hours. Mr. Seselj, you'd like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to draw your attention to the following: However irrelevant the Council of Europe may be with respect to this Tribunal, the United Nations are relevant indeed, and by a decision of the Security Council, the United Nations have decided that all first instance trials have to be finished by the 31st of December 2008. This decision is still in force. There has been no other decision. This is almost equivalent to the statute of the Tribunal. So this should be borne in mind and the Prosecution should bear this in mind when planning their time and also take into account of the time that I will need. So everything has to be done and the judgement handed down by the 31st of December. That's how things stand legally. We cannot work under the assumption that things will change. That would not be legal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think everybody would agree to the fact that this trial should end by December 2008. Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You had mentioned last Status Conference that you were intending to make a trip to the Detention Unit next week and I was wondering if those provisions have been finalised because we would like to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had prepared all this and I had prepared a protocol also, but I think that the purpose of this is to go and visit Mr. Seselj where he is working, which is the adjacent cell to see whether he has everything he needs. The shelves and everything else, as the documents -- no, as everything is still under way, I don't think the visit would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The documents haven't all been sent yet so I don't think it's appropriate to go and visit Mr. Seselj now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be more appropriate to go and visit him in August after the summer recess. So you are just now providing a new piece of information, namely the Prosecution would also like to come along, but this raises a problem because the Prosecution may not look at the defence strategy of the accused, because much may depend on which way the binders are organised in his room, for instance. It's as if Mr. Seselj would file a motion to go and visit your office. Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I'm not opposed to Madam Dahl coming and visiting my working area. I will organise my files in such a manner that she will be able to understand nothing so that would not be any threat to me. But this is not yet finished. Holes have been drilled in the walls. There are shelves there. The painting has started but there is no indication as to when this will be finished. This was not my initiative, it was yours, I'm very glad that you want to visit. If Ms. Dahl also wants to visit I will not object and I will receive her with pleasure and believe me, they will not be able to uncover any secret of mine. I'm a seasoned conspirator from my anti-communist times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj has nothing against you coming to visit him in the detention centre. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall meet again, as I have said, on the 17th of August. As you have realised, I try to do everything I can to settle a great number of issues. We haven't been able to settle them all. I thank you for the spirit in which all of this has unfolded today, and we shall meet again on the 17th of August. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
